In white patients, these disorders include cystic fibrosis, Tay-Sachs disease, and spinal muscular atrophy. Cystic fibrosis carrier state increases the risk that the child may have the disorder if the father is either a carrier or affected. questionStem: A 16-year-old girl comes to the office because she has not had a menstrual period in 2 months. Menses previously occurred at regular 30-day intervals. One month ago, she was diagnosed with rubella; the symptoms resolved spontaneously. She has no other history of serious illness and takes no medications. She is sexually active with one male partner; they use condoms inconsistently. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with an 11-week gestation. A urine pregnancy test is positive. This patient's fetus is at greatest risk for which of the following cardiac disorders?
correctExplanation: Congenital rubella presents with the classic triad of cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and congenital heart disease. Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and pulmonary artery stenosis are the most common cardiac defects. The ductus arteriosus (DA) is one of several physiologic shunts existing during the prenatal period. In utero, oxygenated blood is obtained from the placenta, not from the lungs, and the DA allows the shunting of oxygenated blood from the pulmonary artery directly to the aorta while bypassing the fetal lungs, which are filled with amniotic fluid. At birth, closure of the DA occurs by the release of prostaglandins and increased arterial oxygen tension. With increased blood oxygenation and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance following birth or with indomethacin use, prostaglandin production falls and the ductus closes. PDA presents with a heart murmur described as a continuous “machine-like” murmur best heard in the left second intercostal and left infraclavicular regions. Since blood flow through the PDA occurs in both systole and diastole, the sound will be present throughout the cardiac cycle. Certain congenital heart diseases require the presence of a shunt to allow arteriovenous admixture of oxygenated blood, for example, transposition of the great vessels. In the absence of such a requirement for shunting, a PDA results in a chronic extracardiac left-to-right shunt that may result in pulmonary hypertension or right-sided heart failure, with the risk for Eisenmenger syndrome if uncorrected. PDAs that are small often go undetected until adulthood because the left-to-right shunt is not significant enough to cause symptoms. Caused by a point mutation in the F5 gene of factor V, it is the most common inherited cause of hypercoagulability in white patients. Pregnancy causes a hypercoagulable state due to the overexpression of coagulation factors |, Il, VII, VIII, IX, and X, the underexpression of anticoagulant protein S, and venous stasis in the pelvis and lower extremities caused by hormonal changes and compression by the gravid uterus. A heritable coagulation disorder should be suspected in this patient with a history of provoked deep venous thrombosis (DVT) in combination with an extensive family history of thromboembolic events.
